title: Nation Builder: The Path to Prosperity
description: Guide your nation from a small settlement to a prosperous civilization. Make policy decisions about education, healthcare, economy, and defense to lead your people to greatness.
learning_objectives: Understand the fundamentals of policy making and how government decisions affect citizens
Learn about resource allocation and the trade-offs involved in national budgeting
Explore core civics concepts including governance, public welfare, and democratic institutions
Analyze economic trade-offs between short-term gains and long-term national prosperity
Develop critical thinking about balancing competing priorities like defense, education, and healthcare

how_to_play.title: How to Play
steps: Roll the dice to advance your nation along the 20-tile civilization journey board
Land on Policy Decision tiles to make critical choices about education, healthcare, economy, and infrastructure
Visit the Treasury tiles to allocate your national budget across key sectors
Face National Crisis tiles where you must answer civics and policy questions to protect your nation
Race AI rival leaders to reach the Prosperity tile with the highest approval rating, GDP, and citizen welfare
tips: Balance spending across all sectors -- neglecting any one area leads to national instability
Investing in education pays off slowly but yields the highest long-term returns for your nation
Keep a reserve fund for emergencies -- natural disasters and economic downturns strike without warning
Pay attention to citizen happiness -- a prosperous economy means nothing if the people are unhappy

evt_education_policy.title: Education Policy: The Future of Your People
evt_education_policy.story: Your nation's literacy rate is just 45%. Advisors present three approaches to education reform. Each has different costs, timelines, and impacts. The choice you make today shapes your nation's workforce and innovation capacity for decades to come. What policy do you implement?

choices.label: Fund universal free public education for all citizens
choices.feedback: Bold and transformative! Free public education costs heavily upfront, but within a generation, your literacy rate soars to 90%. An educated population drives innovation, attracts foreign investment, and strengthens democratic participation. Countries like South Korea and Finland prove that heavy investment in education produces economic miracles. Lesson: Education is the single most powerful engine of long-term national prosperity.

choices.label: Offer tax breaks to private schools to expand access
choices.feedback: A market-driven approach. Private schools expand quickly, but quality varies wildly and fees keep education out of reach for the poorest families. Wealthy districts thrive while rural areas lag behind. Inequality grows. Within 10 years, your literacy rate reaches 65% -- better, but uneven. Lesson: Private sector involvement in education works best alongside strong public investment. Markets alone do not ensure equal opportunity.

choices.label: Keep education spending minimal -- focus budget elsewhere
choices.feedback: Short-sighted and costly in the long run. Without educated workers, your nation cannot build competitive industries. Brain drain accelerates as talented citizens emigrate for better opportunities abroad. Innovation stagnates. Within 20 years, your economy falls behind nations that invested in their people. Lesson: Cutting education spending saves money today but bankrupts your nation's future.

evt_healthcare_reform.title: Healthcare Reform: The Wellbeing of Your People
evt_healthcare_reform.story: A disease outbreak has exposed your nation's fragile healthcare system. Only 30% of citizens have access to basic medical care. Hospitals are overcrowded, and rural areas have almost no doctors. Your health minister presents three reform options. The decisions you make will determine whether your citizens live healthy, productive lives.

choices.label: Establish a universal public healthcare system
choices.feedback: A transformative decision! Universal healthcare means every citizen -- rich or poor -- can see a doctor without going bankrupt. Life expectancy jumps. Worker productivity rises because healthy people work better. Countries like the UK (NHS) and India (Ayushman Bharat) show that public healthcare, despite its costs, creates a healthier and more equal society. Lesson: A nation's greatest asset is its people's health. Universal healthcare is an investment, not an expense.

choices.label: Create a government-subsidized insurance scheme
choices.feedback: A pragmatic middle ground. Government-subsidized insurance covers major illnesses while keeping costs manageable. However, the poorest citizens still struggle with premiums and out-of-pocket costs for routine care. Coverage reaches 60% of the population. Lesson: Insurance-based systems reduce catastrophic health costs but can still leave gaps for the most vulnerable. Complementary programs are needed.

choices.label: Let the private sector handle healthcare -- no government role
choices.feedback: Profit-driven healthcare creates world-class hospitals for the wealthy and nothing for the poor. Medical costs skyrocket. Citizens go into debt for basic treatments. The disease outbreak worsens in underserved communities, eventually spreading to wealthier areas too. Lesson: Healthcare is not a luxury good. When governments leave healthcare entirely to the market, public health collapses and inequality explodes.

evt_trade_agreement.title: International Trade Agreement
evt_trade_agreement.story: A powerful neighboring nation proposes a trade deal. They will buy your agricultural products at premium prices, but in return they want you to open your markets to their manufactured goods. Your local manufacturers are worried about competition, but farmers are excited about new export opportunities. How do you negotiate?

choices.label: Negotiate a balanced deal with protections for key industries
choices.feedback: Excellent diplomacy! You open agricultural exports while negotiating tariff protections for infant industries that need time to grow. Farmers prosper, and local manufacturers get a 5-year window to become competitive. This is how nations like Japan and South Korea industrialized -- strategic trade policy that opens markets gradually. Lesson: Smart trade policy balances openness with protection. Free trade is powerful, but strategic industries sometimes need time to develop.

choices.label: Accept fully open trade -- complete free market
choices.feedback: GDP surges from cheap imports and export revenue, but local manufacturers collapse under foreign competition. Unemployment spikes in industrial cities. Your nation becomes dependent on imports for manufactured goods, making you vulnerable if the trade partner ever imposes sanctions. Lesson: Unrestricted free trade creates winners and losers. Without transition support for affected workers and industries, the social costs can outweigh the economic gains.

choices.label: Reject the deal -- protect domestic industries at all costs
choices.feedback: Your manufacturers cheer, but farmers lose a lucrative export market. Without competition, domestic companies become complacent and inefficient. Consumer prices rise because there are no cheap imports. The neighboring nation signs the deal with your rival instead, gaining an economic advantage. Lesson: Pure protectionism stifles innovation and raises costs for consumers. No nation has prospered by shutting itself off from global trade entirely.

evt_defense_budget.title: Defense Budget: Guns or Butter?
evt_defense_budget.story: Your military generals demand a 40% increase in the defense budget, citing threats from neighboring nations. But your education minister argues that the money would be better spent on schools, and your health minister wants more hospitals. Your treasury has limited funds. This is the classic 'guns vs butter' dilemma that every nation faces. How do you allocate resources?

choices.label: Moderate defense increase (15%), invest the rest in social programs
choices.feedback: A statesman's choice! A moderate defense increase maintains deterrence without starving social programs. History shows that nations with educated, healthy populations are stronger in the long run than those with oversized militaries but struggling citizens. Israel spends heavily on defense but also invests massively in education and technology. Lesson: National security includes economic strength, social cohesion, and an educated populace -- not just military hardware.

choices.label: Grant the full 40% increase -- national security comes first
choices.feedback: Your military is now formidable, but schools close, hospitals are understaffed, and infrastructure crumbles. Citizens grow resentful of a government that prioritizes tanks over textbooks. The Soviet Union collapsed not from military weakness but because it spent so much on defense that its economy and society hollowed out. Lesson: Excessive military spending at the expense of human development weakens a nation from within. The greatest threat is often internal, not external.

choices.label: Slash the defense budget entirely -- invest everything in welfare
choices.feedback: Citizens love the new schools and hospitals, but neighboring nations notice your weakened military. Border incursions increase. Trade partners lose confidence in your stability. Without basic security, even your social programs are at risk. Costa Rica abolished its military in 1948 -- but it works because of strong alliances and a unique geographic position. Most nations do not have that luxury. Lesson: Some level of defense is essential for sovereignty. The question is finding the right balance.

evt_infrastructure.title: Infrastructure Plan: Building the Nation's Backbone
evt_infrastructure.story: Your nation's roads are poor, internet connectivity is limited to cities, and rural villages lack clean water and electricity. An ambitious infrastructure plan could transform the country, but it requires massive investment. Your advisors present three approaches to building infrastructure.

choices.label: Launch a comprehensive national infrastructure program
choices.feedback: A nation-building masterstroke! New roads connect rural farmers to urban markets, cutting food costs by 30%. Internet connectivity enables remote education and telemedicine. Clean water reduces disease. GDP growth accelerates as businesses can now operate efficiently nationwide. India's Golden Quadrilateral highway project transformed its economy. Lesson: Infrastructure is the foundation upon which all other progress is built. Without roads, power, and connectivity, even the best policies cannot reach citizens.

choices.label: Focus infrastructure spending on major cities only
choices.feedback: Cities boom with new metro lines, high-speed internet, and modern utilities. But rural areas are left behind. Mass migration to cities causes overcrowding, slums, and social tension. The urban-rural divide deepens, creating two separate nations within one border. Lesson: City-focused development creates economic hubs but can worsen inequality. Inclusive infrastructure that reaches all citizens builds a stronger, more unified nation.

choices.label: Delay infrastructure spending -- the economy is not ready
choices.feedback: Every year of delay costs more. Roads deteriorate further, making repairs more expensive. Businesses relocate to neighboring countries with better infrastructure. Foreign investors pass on your nation. The cost of inaction compounds. Lesson: Delaying infrastructure investment is itself a costly decision. Crumbling infrastructure acts as a hidden tax on the entire economy.

evt_environment.title: Environmental Policy: Growth vs Green
evt_environment.story: Your nation's rapid industrialization has polluted rivers, deforested vast areas, and worsened air quality in cities. Scientists warn that continuing on this path will cause irreversible environmental damage within a decade. But industry leaders argue that strict environmental regulations will slow economic growth and cost jobs. What is your environmental policy?

choices.label: Implement strict environmental regulations with green energy transition
choices.feedback: Short-term economic adjustment, long-term prosperity! Clean air and water improve public health, reducing healthcare costs. Green energy industries create new high-skilled jobs. Your nation becomes a leader in renewable energy exports. Germany's Energiewende (energy transition) shows that going green can drive innovation and economic growth. Lesson: Environmental protection and economic growth are not opposites. Sustainable development creates a competitive advantage for the future.

choices.label: Set gradual targets -- reduce pollution by 30% over 10 years
choices.feedback: A pragmatic approach. Gradual targets give industries time to adapt without sudden job losses. Pollution decreases slowly. Some environmental damage is locked in, but the worst outcomes are avoided. This middle path works if targets are actually enforced -- many nations set targets but fail to follow through. Lesson: Gradual environmental action is better than none, but only if enforcement is strong. The danger is that 'gradual' becomes 'never.'

choices.label: No restrictions -- prioritize industrial growth at all costs
choices.feedback: GDP spikes, but at a devastating cost. Rivers become too toxic for drinking. Air pollution causes a spike in respiratory diseases, costing more in healthcare than the economic gains. Farmland degrades, threatening food security. Within 15 years, the environmental cleanup costs are 10 times what regulation would have cost. Lesson: Ignoring the environment is borrowing from the future. The bill always comes due -- with interest.

evt_democratic_reform.title: Democratic Reform: Power to the People?
evt_democratic_reform.story: Citizens are demanding more say in how the nation is governed. Protests call for free press, independent judiciary, and local self-governance. Some advisors warn that too much democracy slows decision-making. Others argue that democratic accountability prevents corruption and tyranny. How do you respond to the people's demands?

choices.label: Embrace full democratic reforms -- free press, independent courts, local governance
choices.feedback: A courageous choice! Democratic institutions slow some decisions, but they also prevent catastrophic ones. A free press exposes corruption, saving billions. Independent courts protect citizens' rights and attract foreign investors who trust the rule of law. Local governance ensures policies match local needs. India's democratic system, despite its messy complexity, has provided stability and peaceful transitions of power for over 75 years. Lesson: Democracy is not efficient, but it is resilient. Accountable governments build trust and long-term stability.

choices.label: Allow some reforms but keep central control over key decisions
choices.feedback: A controlled opening. You allow a semi-free press and advisory local councils but retain central authority over economic and security policy. This model works in the short term -- efficient decisions and some accountability. But without full transparency, corruption can fester in the shadows. Citizens grow frustrated with half-measures. Lesson: Partial reforms can be a stepping stone or a trap. The key is whether they lead to more openness over time or become a permanent ceiling.

choices.label: Reject reforms -- strong centralized leadership is more effective
choices.feedback: Efficiency without accountability is a dangerous combination. Decisions are made quickly but without checks, mistakes go uncorrected and corruption flourishes. The press is silenced, so problems are hidden until they become crises. Citizens lose trust in institutions. History is littered with 'efficient' authoritarian states that collapsed suddenly. Lesson: Centralized power can deliver fast growth but at the cost of freedom and resilience. Without democratic checks, even well-meaning leaders make unchallenged mistakes.

evt_technology.title: Technology Initiative: The Digital Leap
evt_technology.story: The world is going digital and your nation risks falling behind. Only 15% of citizens have internet access. Your technology minister proposes a national digital initiative: broadband for all, digital identity systems, e-governance, and support for tech startups. But rural leaders worry about digital exclusion, and privacy advocates raise concerns about government surveillance.

choices.label: Launch inclusive digital program with privacy protections
choices.feedback: Masterful execution! India's Aadhaar and Digital India programs show how digital identity and connectivity can revolutionize governance -- direct benefit transfers eliminate middlemen, e-governance reduces corruption, and digital literacy opens global opportunities even for rural citizens. Strong privacy laws (like GDPR) build citizen trust. Your tech startup ecosystem flourishes. Lesson: Technology amplifies whatever system it is applied to. With good governance and privacy protections, digital transformation is a massive equalizer.

choices.label: Focus digital initiative on cities and tech hubs only
choices.feedback: Your cities become tech powerhouses with thriving startup scenes, but a digital divide emerges. Rural citizens are locked out of e-governance services, digital banking, and online education. The gap between connected urban citizens and disconnected rural ones becomes a new form of inequality. Lesson: Technology can either bridge divides or deepen them. Digital programs that exclude large portions of the population create a two-tier society.

choices.label: Avoid digitization -- traditional systems work fine
choices.feedback: While your nation clings to paper-based systems, neighboring countries leapfrog ahead. Government services remain slow, corrupt middlemen thrive, and your brightest young minds emigrate to countries offering digital opportunities. Within a decade, your economy is globally uncompetitive. Lesson: Resisting technological change does not preserve the status quo -- it guarantees decline. Every industrial revolution has rewarded adapters and punished resisters.

evt_boss_recession.title: National Crisis: Economic Recession!
evt_boss_recession.story: Global commodity prices crash and your economy plunges into recession. GDP contracts, unemployment doubles, and tax revenues collapse. Your finance minister presents emergency options. The wrong response could deepen the crisis for years. What is the correct economic response to a recession?

choices.label: Launch a government stimulus: increase spending to create jobs and demand
choices.feedback: CORRECT! Keynesian economics in action. During a recession, private spending collapses, so the government steps in to create demand -- building infrastructure, funding public works, and providing safety nets. This prevents a downward spiral where layoffs lead to less spending, which leads to more layoffs. India's MGNREGA program and the US New Deal are examples of stimulus that helped economies recover. Lesson: In a recession, government spending acts as a shock absorber. Austerity during a downturn deepens the crisis.

choices.label: Cut government spending drastically -- balance the budget at all costs
choices.feedback: WRONG! Austerity during a recession is like taking away a patient's medicine because they are already sick. Cutting spending reduces demand further, increases unemployment, and shrinks tax revenues -- making the deficit worse, not better. Greece's austerity measures after 2008 shrank its economy by 25% and caused a humanitarian crisis. Lesson: Balancing the budget is important in good times, but during a recession, cutting spending deepens the downturn.

choices.label: Print unlimited money to solve the problem
choices.feedback: DANGEROUS! Unlimited money printing causes hyperinflation -- where prices double every few months. Your currency becomes worthless. Zimbabwe in 2008 and Venezuela in 2018 show what happens when governments print money without restraint -- citizens need wheelbarrows of cash to buy bread. Controlled monetary policy (central bank interest rate cuts) can help, but printing unlimited money is economic suicide. Lesson: There is a difference between smart monetary policy and reckless money printing. Central bank independence matters.

evt_boss_disaster.title: National Crisis: Devastating Flood!
evt_boss_disaster.story: Catastrophic flooding hits your nation's most populous region. Rivers burst their banks, displacing 2 million people. Homes are destroyed, crops are ruined, and disease threatens to spread in overcrowded relief camps. Your disaster management agency is overwhelmed. How do you respond?

choices.label: Activate national emergency: coordinate military, NGOs, and international aid
choices.feedback: CORRECT! A coordinated multi-agency response is the gold standard for disaster management. Military provides logistics and rescue. NGOs handle relief camps and medical aid. International organizations bring expertise and resources. Japan's disaster response system -- one of the world's best -- works because of precise coordination between agencies, early warning systems, and pre-positioned supplies. Lesson: Disaster preparedness and coordination save more lives than reactive spending. Invest in emergency infrastructure before disasters strike.

choices.label: Just send money to the affected region and let locals handle it
choices.feedback: WRONG! Money without coordination leads to chaos. Relief funds are stolen by corrupt middlemen. Supplies pile up in warehouses while citizens starve miles away. Without organized distribution, the same community gets aid twice while another gets nothing. The aftermath of many poorly managed disasters shows that money alone does not save lives. Lesson: Effective disaster response requires logistics, coordination, and accountability -- not just funding.

choices.label: Downplay the crisis to avoid panic and economic damage
choices.feedback: CATASTROPHIC! Downplaying the crisis delays rescue operations, allowing preventable deaths. Citizens lose trust in the government. International aid is not requested in time. Disease spreads unchecked in relief camps. When the true scale of destruction eventually emerges, public outrage is volcanic. Lesson: Transparency during crisis is not optional. Citizens deserve accurate information, and hiding the truth makes every outcome worse.

evt_boss_border_conflict.title: National Crisis: Border Conflict Escalation!
evt_boss_border_conflict.story: Tensions with a neighboring nation escalate after a border incident. Their troops have occupied a disputed territory. Hawks in your cabinet demand a military response. Doves push for diplomatic negotiation. The international community is watching. A wrong move could trigger a devastating war or embolden the aggressor. What is the wisest approach?

choices.label: Pursue firm diplomacy: negotiate from strength while avoiding escalation
choices.feedback: CORRECT! The best leaders are firm but measured. You mobilize troops to the border (showing strength) while simultaneously opening diplomatic channels and involving international mediators. This approach -- called 'coercive diplomacy' -- signals that you will fight if necessary but prefer a peaceful resolution. The Cuban Missile Crisis was resolved exactly this way. Lesson: In international conflicts, the goal is to protect your interests without unnecessary destruction. Strong diplomacy backed by credible military capability is the most effective approach.

choices.label: Launch an immediate full military offensive
choices.feedback: WRONG! War is devastatingly expensive in blood and treasure. Even if you win the battle, the economic cost is staggering -- military operations drain the treasury, trade is disrupted, foreign investors flee, and reconstruction costs are enormous. Civilian casualties erode international support. Most modern border conflicts that escalated into full war left both sides worse off. Lesson: War should always be the last resort, not the first response. The economic, human, and diplomatic costs of war almost always exceed the value of what is being fought over.

choices.label: Immediately concede the territory to avoid any conflict
choices.feedback: WRONG! Unconditional surrender emboldens the aggressor to make more demands. Other neighboring nations see your weakness and press their own territorial claims. Your citizens feel betrayed and lose faith in the government's ability to protect them. History shows that appeasement rarely satisfies aggressors -- they simply want more. Lesson: Avoiding conflict at all costs is as dangerous as seeking conflict at all costs. National sovereignty requires the willingness to defend it, combined with the wisdom to use diplomacy first.

evt_innovation_boom.title: Innovation Boom! Scientific Breakthrough
evt_innovation_boom.story: Your national research institute makes a breakthrough in renewable energy technology! The discovery could position your nation as a global leader in clean energy exports. International companies are offering partnerships, and neighboring nations want to license the technology.

choices.label: Share the technology openly to build international goodwill
choices.feedback: Generous and strategic! Sharing the technology builds powerful alliances and positions your nation as a global leader. Trade partnerships strengthen. Your scientists gain international recognition, attracting more talent to your research institutions. Sometimes the greatest national advantage comes from being the country that others want to work with.

choices.label: Commercialize aggressively -- sell licenses at premium prices
choices.feedback: A profitable approach! License revenue floods the treasury. But some nations develop their own alternatives to avoid paying your fees. Your competitive advantage has a shelf life. The revenue windfall is real but temporary.

evt_cultural_renaissance.title: Cultural Renaissance! Artistic Flourishing
evt_cultural_renaissance.story: Your nation is experiencing a cultural renaissance! Artists, writers, musicians, and filmmakers are gaining international recognition. The world is fascinated by your culture. This soft power can be as valuable as military might. How do you support this cultural moment?

choices.label: Establish a National Arts Fund and cultural exchange programs
choices.feedback: Brilliant investment in soft power! Your films, music, and literature become globally popular, driving tourism and cultural exports. South Korea's investment in cultural industries (K-pop, K-dramas, cinema) generated billions in economic value and made the nation a global cultural powerhouse. Lesson: Culture is a renewable resource that generates economic value and international influence far beyond its cost.

choices.label: Appreciate the moment but focus government funds elsewhere
choices.feedback: The cultural moment fades without institutional support. Artists emigrate to countries that fund the arts. A generation of cultural influence is lost. Tourism remains flat. Lesson: Cultural moments are rare and valuable. Without strategic support, they dissipate. Investing in culture during a renaissance yields outsized returns.

evt_treasury_1.title: First Treasury Visit: Foundation Budget
evt_treasury_1.story: Welcome to the National Treasury! Your nation is young and resources are limited. Your finance minister presents three key investment areas. Each choice shapes your nation's growth trajectory. Choose wisely -- every coin spent here determines your future capabilities.

choices.label: Review the budget allocation options
choices.feedback: Smart leaders study their options before committing resources. Understanding trade-offs is the foundation of good governance.

evt_treasury_2.title: Advanced Treasury: Expansion Budget
evt_treasury_2.story: Your nation has grown and so has the budget! The treasury now offers advanced investment options: technology research grants, international development aid (which builds alliances), or a sovereign wealth fund for future generations.

choices.label: Review the advanced budget options
choices.feedback: As your nation matures, the investment choices become more sophisticated. Long-term thinking separates great nations from merely good ones.

win_conditions.description: Reach the Prosperous Nation tile! Your success is measured by GDP growth, citizen approval rating, welfare improvements, and national knowledge accumulated throughout your leadership journey.

glossary_terms.definition: The total monetary value of all goods and services produced within a nation's borders in a specific time period. It is the most common measure of a country's economic size and health.
glossary_terms.example: India's GDP in 2023 was about $3.7 trillion, making it the 5th largest economy in the world. When GDP grows, it generally means more jobs, more income, and more tax revenue for the government.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: GDP = the nation's total economic scorecard. Growing GDP means a growing economy, but distribution matters too.

glossary_terms.definition: Government decisions about taxation and spending. Expansionary fiscal policy (more spending, lower taxes) stimulates the economy during recessions. Contractionary fiscal policy (less spending, higher taxes) cools down an overheating economy.
glossary_terms.example: During COVID-19, India launched a fiscal stimulus of Rs 20 lakh crore (about 10% of GDP) through the Atmanirbhar Bharat package to support businesses and workers during the lockdown.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Fiscal Policy = the government's wallet decisions. Spend more in bad times, save more in good times.

glossary_terms.definition: A situation where pursuing one benefit requires giving up another. In governance, every policy choice involves trade-offs because resources (money, time, attention) are limited.
glossary_terms.example: Spending more on military means less money for schools. Building a dam provides electricity but may displace communities. Every policy decision has winners, losers, and unintended consequences.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Trade-off = you cannot have everything. Choosing one thing means giving up another. Good leaders make trade-offs transparent.

glossary_terms.definition: The process of distributing limited resources (money, people, materials) among competing needs and priorities. It is the core challenge of governance and economics.
glossary_terms.example: A national budget of Rs 45 lakh crore must be divided among defense (15%), education (3%), healthcare (2%), infrastructure (10%), and dozens of other needs. Changing one allocation affects all others.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Resource Allocation = cutting the national pie. The question is always: who gets how much, and why?

glossary_terms.definition: A system of government where power is vested in the people, who exercise it through elected representatives. Key features include free elections, rule of law, independent judiciary, free press, and protection of minority rights.
glossary_terms.example: India is the world's largest democracy with over 900 million eligible voters. The Constitution guarantees fundamental rights, and power transitions peacefully through elections every 5 years.
glossary_terms.remember_tip: Democracy = government of the people, by the people, for the people. Messy but resilient.

achievements.title: Crisis Commander
achievements.description: Choose the correct option in all 3 National Crisis boss tiles

gdp.definition: The total value of all goods and services produced within a country. The primary measure of economic health.
gdp.example: India's GDP of $3.7 trillion means that's the total value produced in a year.
gdp.real_world_example: China's GDP grew from $150 billion in 1978 to over $17 trillion — the fastest growth in history.

public_policy.definition: Decisions and actions taken by government to address societal issues like healthcare, education, and infrastructure.
public_policy.example: A government deciding to provide free school lunches to improve child nutrition.
public_policy.real_world_example: Finland's education policy produces top global results with no standardized testing.

infrastructure.definition: The fundamental physical systems of a society — roads, bridges, power grids, water systems, and telecom.
infrastructure.example: Building a highway connecting two cities to improve trade.
infrastructure.real_world_example: China built 42,000 km of high-speed rail in 15 years.

diplomacy.definition: The art of managing international relations through negotiation and dialogue rather than force.
diplomacy.example: Two countries resolving a border dispute through talks and a treaty.
diplomacy.real_world_example: The Camp David Accords (1978) achieved peace between Egypt and Israel.

sustainability.definition: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
sustainability.example: Using renewable energy sources like solar and wind instead of coal.
sustainability.real_world_example: Costa Rica generates 99% of its electricity from renewable sources.

governance.definition: The system by which a country, organization, or community is directed and controlled through policies and rules.
governance.example: Creating transparent budgeting processes so citizens can see how taxes are spent.
governance.real_world_example: Singapore's efficient governance transformed it from a developing nation to one of the wealthiest in just 50 years.

win_criteria.label: Best Resource Balance
win_criteria.description: Lowest variance across all resource growth percentages

coaching_moment: Understand the fundamentals of policy making and how government decisions affect citizens. Learn about resource allocation and the trade-offs involved in national budgeting.
cultural_context: India's federal democracy requires its citizens to understand the trade-offs of governance at scale — balancing regional interests, public spending, and national development goals. This game develops that systems perspective.
